extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and patent litigators (attorneys trying patent cases); jurors as recipients of the instructions
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for use in U.S. patent trials, specifying legal standards, definitions, and decision rules the jury must apply (claim construction, infringement types, evidentiary standards, limitations on equivalents, etc.). Intended to guide judges in instructing juries and attorneys in framing issues at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of proof (preponderance, clear and convincing, beyond reasonable doubt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains and contrasts standards of proof: preponderance of the evidence (slightly greater than 50%), clear and convincing (higher than preponderance but below beyond a reasonable doubt), and beyond a reasonable doubt (approaching certainty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: When the instruction uses the phrase 'clear and convincing', consider substituting explanatory language such as 'highly probable' to help jurors understand and apply the standard. Courts/practitioners should decide case-by-case whether substitute language is helpful. (Cites Addington v. Texas; Colorado v. New Mexico for guidance on explaining 'clear-and-convincing'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial procedure phases and evidence rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial consists of six phases (voir dire, opening statements, evidence presentation, closing arguments, jury instructions, deliberation/verdict). Opening and closing statements are not evidence; jurors must decide based only on admitted evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that evidence may be presented piecemeal and jurors should keep an open mind until all evidence is in. Describe sequence: plaintiff calls witnesses first; direct then cross-examination; testimony may be live, by deposition transcript, or videotape (deposition entitled to same consideration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the scope of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims are the numbered sentences at the end of the patent that define the invention and the patent owner's exclusive rights; only claims can be infringed (not the written description or drawings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim must be considered individually. The words of the claims define the scope of exclusive rights, and the same claim meaning must be used for infringement and invalidity determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's role in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge will determine the meaning of claim language that must be interpreted and will provide those meanings to the jury; the jury must accept and use the court's constructions when deciding infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read any stipulations and the court's constructions aloud. Citations: Teva; Phillips; Markman family of cases. Emphasize jury must follow judge's claim meanings even if they disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutoff Date (pre-AIA vs AIA) and prior art pool
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines Cutoff Date: pre-AIA law may have different Cutoff Dates depending on subsection of §102; under the AIA the Cutoff Date is the effective filing date of the claimed invention. Different claims in a patent may have different Cutoff Dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims have different Cutoff Dates and those dates are disputed, the jury may need instructions on how to determine the Cutoff Date(s) and on differences in the pool of available prior art for each claim. Practice Note explains pre-AIA variances (date of invention or one year before filing/effective priority) and AIA definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: person of ordinary skill in the art (pre-AIA/AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary skill in the art refers to the level of experience, education, or training generally possessed by those working in the area of the invention at the relevant time (time of invention pre-AIA; before the effective filing date under AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the perspective for various analyses (e.g., equivalence in means-plus-function claims, obviousness analyses elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement—burden and mental state immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant is liable for direct infringement if the plaintiff proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim during the patent term. Knowledge of the patent or intent to infringe is immaterial to direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) and cases (Commil, Medtronic, Global-Tech, etc.). Instruction emphasizes the 'more likely than not' standard for direct infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement—all claim elements must be present
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product or method includes each and every element (or method step) recited in that patent claim, applying the court's claim constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine literal infringement separately for each asserted claim. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element. If any element is missing, there is no literal infringement. (Cites cases such as Limelight, Hutchins, Gen. Mills.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under claim transitional language ('comprising'/'consisting of'/'consisting essentially of')
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains meanings of common transitional phrases in claim preambles: 'comprising' means including the following but not excluding others; 'consisting of' means including the following and excluding others; 'consisting essentially of' means including the following and possibly unlisted components that do not materially affect the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accused product/method includes all claim elements but also additional components, 'comprising' still permits literal infringement; 'consisting of' would preclude literal infringement if additional components exist; 'consisting essentially of' permits additional components only if they do not materially affect the invention. (Cites relevant case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement—joint infringement (attribution rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant can directly infringe even if multiple parties perform different steps of a claimed method, if the steps performed by another party are attributable to the defendant (either because the defendant exercised direction or control over the other party or because the parties formed a joint enterprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant did not personally perform all acts and steps are not attributable under direction/control or joint enterprise, then no direct infringement. Joint enterprise requires proof of four elements: (1) agreement among group members; (2) common purpose; (3) community of pecuniary interest; and (4) equal right to a voice in direction (equal right of control). Practice Note: Joint infringement and inducement can be confusing—consider presenting them together to clarify differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function and step-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish literal infringement of a means-plus-function or step-plus-function limitation, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused product/method (1) performs the recited function, and (2) includes structure or step that is identical or equivalent to the corresponding structure/step described in the patent specification/drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First decide whether the accused product/method has any structure/step that performs the specific function; if not, no infringement of that limitation. If it does, determine whether that structure/step is the same as or equivalent to the structure recited in the specification. Equivalence is decided from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art; insubstantial differences or performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result are indicators of equivalence. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112 and Federal Circuit authority (Williamson, Brilliant Instruments, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim incorporates all elements of the independent claim to which it refers; to establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, the plaintiff must prove the accused product/method includes every element of both the independent and dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the independent claim is not literally infringed, the dependent claim cannot be literally infringed. Explain independent vs dependent claim structure with examples. (Cites Wahpeton Canvas, Shatterproof Glass.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents—when to apply and equivalence tests
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe, the jury must decide whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents by having components/steps equivalent to missing claim elements. Equivalence can be shown by demonstrating an element is insubstantially different from the claimed element or that it performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury may consider whether persons of ordinary skill at the time would have known of interchangeability, though known interchangeability is not required. If a claim is literally infringed, no need to resort to the doctrine of equivalents; the doctrine is available only if one or more claim elements are not literally met. The same accused component may satisfy more than one claim element, and multiple accused components may together satisfy a single claim element. (Cites Warner-Jenkinson, Graver Tank.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents—prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel can bar application of the doctrine of equivalents for claim elements surrendered during prosecution by argument or amendment made for reasons related to patentability; if the court determines prosecution history estoppel applies, the jury should be instructed that the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to specified claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction should be given only if the court has determined prosecution history estoppel applies as a matter of law. The court should list the elements on a claim-by-claim basis for which equivalents are barred; those elements must be literally present for infringement. (Cites Festo and related authority.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents—dedication to the public (subject matter dedication)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court determines, as a matter of law, that certain subject matter has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those claim elements; those elements must be literally present for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction should be given only if the court has made the dedication-to-public determination. The court should list the elements on a claim-by-claim basis that cannot be found by equivalents. (Cites SanDisk, Pfizer, PSC Computer Prods., Toro, Johnson & Johnston.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice note: Distinguish theories of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid jury confusion, distinguish claims alleged to be infringed directly versus indirectly, literal infringement versus doctrine of equivalents, and induced infringement versus contributory infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider presenting related instructions (e.g., joint infringement and inducement) back-to-back and in a way that highlights differences in theories, required evidence, and specific findings jurors must make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of testimony and weight of depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony may be presented live, by reading deposition transcript, or by playing videotaped deposition; a deposition is sworn testimony taken before trial and is entitled to the same consideration as if the witness testified at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors that all three forms are acceptable and should be considered equally when weighing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active inducement (introductory instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduces the separate theory of active inducement (indirect infringement) as distinct from direct infringement and joint infringement, and notes potential jury confusion between these concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: If both joint infringement and inducement instructions are given, consider instructing them back-to-back to enable jurors to appreciate differences in the theories and evidence required. (Full inducement instruction appears elsewhere in the model instructions.)
